extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners and patent office staff in ASEAN member states
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting prior-art searches and assessing novelty (and related requirements) for patent applications in ASEAN Member States, including search strategy, search report content, determination of closest prior art, and novelty tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of cited documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents cited in the application should be examined if they are cited as the starting point of the invention, show the state of the art, are alternative solutions to the problem, or are necessary for a correct understanding of the application; citations that clearly relate only to details not directly relevant to the claimed invention may be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine cited documents when they affect understanding or claim scope; disregard citations only when clearly irrelevant to the claimed invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requesting inaccessible cited documents
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application cites a document not published or not accessible to the searching authority and that document appears essential to a correct understanding of the invention, the searching authority may request the applicant to provide a copy if possible within time limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no copy is received, attempt the search and, if necessary, indicate that a meaningful search could not be carried out or needed to be restricted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of abstract and title
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should consider the abstract together with the title and figure(s) to be published; since the abstract should relate to the application as filed, the examiner should determine its definitive contents no later than the completion of the search report.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finalize abstract contents by the time the search report is completed; use abstract/title/figure to help define subject matter for search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification according to IPC
rubrics_metrics.description: After considering the abstract, the examiner should classify the application according to at least the International Patent Classification (IPC).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use IPC classification to guide search strategy and placement in classification places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search statement (defining subject of search)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner may prepare a written search statement defining the subject of their search as precisely as possible; claims may serve but might need generalisation to cover embodiments. Exclusion from search and lack of unity should be borne in mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where unity lacking, examiner may search only the first invention or inventive concept; restrict search only in exceptional situations where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restriction of search only in exceptional situations
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner may have to restrict the search in exceptional situations because no search at all is possible, but they should not do this if it can be avoided.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid restricting searches unless unavoidable; consider partial searches as alternative where unity objections or other limitations apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of claim types/forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be construed and searched having particular regard to the various types and forms of claims used, such as two-part claims and product-by-process claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate interpretive/search approaches depending on claim format (e.g., two-part, product-by-process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the closest prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The closest prior art is that which in one single reference discloses the combination of features which constitutes the most promising starting point for a development leading to the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select closest prior art directed to a similar purpose/effect or from same/closely related technical field and capable of carrying out the claimed function; examiner selection based on claim interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search focus on documents affecting novelty, inventive step, and sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner carries out the search directing attention to any prior art likely to have bearing on novelty or inventive step and is encouraged to cite prior art likely to assist in determining sufficiency of description and support.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize documents that affect novelty, inventive step, adequacy of support, and industrial applicability throughout the claimed field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Noting documents important for other reasons
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should note documents that may be of importance for other reasons (e.g., documents throwing doubt on validity of priority, contributing to understanding, or illustrating technological background), but should not spend time searching for these unless there is a special reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record but do not exhaustively search for background/priority-doubt documents unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of post-dating documents for universal facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents which do not qualify as prior art because they post-date the claimed invention may nevertheless be cited to show a universal fact (e.g., material properties, scientific facts, or level of ordinary skill).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite post-dated documents only to prove general facts, not as novelty-destroying prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concentrate search efforts on most promising resources
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner should concentrate search efforts on resources and strategies in which the probability of finding highly relevant documents is greatest, and identify all documents, regardless of publication dates, that are highly relevant to novelty, inventive step, support, and industrial applicability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take account of search results already obtained when considering whether to extend the search (e.g., additional databases, broaden queries, additional classification places).

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of searching patent vs. non-patent literature
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner typically first conducts a search of the patent literature; in certain art areas (identified in Search Guidance IPDL) non-patent literature may be necessary; if little or no relevant patent prior art is located, consider broadening to non-patent databases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not neglect non-patent literature where patent literature is sparse or the field requires it.

rubrics_metrics.name: No special search for instantly well-known features
rubrics_metrics.description: No special search should be made for features that are instantly and unquestionably demonstrable as being well known such that documentary evidence is unnecessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preferably cite a handbook or other document showing general knowledge if practicable, but do not expend undue search effort on unquestioned common general knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of novelty and inventive step
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner determines whether the claimed invention meets the standards for novelty and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use identified prior art and legal tests to assess novelty and inventive step as separate requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contents required in a search report
rubrics_metrics.description: The search report should include at least: list and details of prior arts identified, date of first publication/availability and weblink when available; scope of the patent search; databases used; classification (IPC); summary of the search; relevance of prior art(s) to the claim(s); comments or written opinion from the examiner on patentability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure search report documents key bibliographic details, relevance assessments, and examiner opinions to support downstream examination and applicant awareness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Partial search / no-search options and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Options for a partial search and/or a 'no search' are available in some AMS. The aim is to issue search reports as complete as possible; no meaningful search should be limited to exceptional situations where no search is possible (e.g., totally unclear description/claims/drawings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meaningful search must be complete enough to determine novelty, inventive step, industrial applicability, sufficiency, support and clarity; where parts are non-compliant but understandable, perform a search and account for non-compliance when determining extent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal definition of novelty (PCT approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is novel if it is not anticipated by prior art. PCT Guidelines: 'The invention, as defined by a claim, lacks novelty if every element or step is explicitly or inherently disclosed within the prior art including any features implicit to a person skilled in the art.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty by checking whether every claim element is explicitly or implicitly disclosed in a single prior-art reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of the state of the art (what counts as prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: The state of the art includes everything made available to the public anywhere in the world before the relevant date by written disclosure (including drawings), use, oral disclosure, or any other way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider global disclosures regardless of language, location, or manner; be mindful of national definitions and policies that may affect what counts as disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for determining claimed-invention scope using PSIA
rubrics_metrics.description: To determine whether an invention is new, the examiner shall compare the claimed invention to identified prior art through the lens of the Person Skilled In the Art (PSIA), applying successive steps: (i) evaluate elements of the claimed invention; (ii) determine if a prior art forms part of the state of the art; (iii) assess whether each and every element or step was explicitly or inherently disclosed in combination to a PSIA on the prior-art date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret claims using description and drawings as needed; if every element is disclosed, novelty is lacking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consideration of purpose/intended use in claim interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: In interpreting claims for novelty consideration, regard should be had to the purpose or intended use of the invention to determine whether the recited purpose results in a structural difference; non-distinctive characteristics of use should be disregarded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: substance X claimed as catalyst not novel over same substance known as dye unless the use implies distinguishing form (e.g., additives); implied characteristics from intended use should be taken into account.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absolute (universal) novelty and grace periods
rubrics_metrics.description: Generally universal/absolute novelty is required: claims must be novel compared to any prior art published or used anywhere. All AMS except Thailand apply 'absolute novelty'. AMS provide a grace period preventing some disclosures from becoming prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty against all worldwide disclosures before the relevant date, subject to applicable grace periods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet disclosures as prior art and date assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet or online database disclosures are treated the same as other written disclosures; password protection or paywalls do not necessarily prevent a webpage from forming part of the state of the art. Establishing publication date requires separate assessment of date and public availability; absent contrary indication, dates may be accepted at face value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant contests publication date, examiner must consider reasons; reliability of internet disclosures varies and the burden to rebut dates is on applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implicit/inherent disclosure as novelty-destroying
rubrics_metrics.description: The disclosure of an invention in the prior art may be implicit/inherent in a prior art document; implicit teachings can be considered part of the prior art and destroy novelty, but lack of novelty based on implicit teaching should be raised only where there can be no reasonable doubt as to the practical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply inherent-disclosure doctrine cautiously; only when PSIA would inevitably arrive at claimed result when carrying out prior teaching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment of technical equivalents
rubrics_metrics.description: Novelty assessment involves whether the prior art discloses each and every feature specified in the claim. If the claim contains technically equivalent or additional features, objection of obviousness may be more appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where equivalents are at issue, consider obviousness rather than novelty in jurisdictions that have guidelines on this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-prejudicial disclosures (exceptions to state of the art)
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures are not part of the state of the art if: (a) they occurred within a specified period preceding filing and resulted from acts by the inventor/applicant (grace); (b) resulted from abuse of rights of the inventor/applicant; (c) information was contained in an application disclosed mistakenly by the Patent Office.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check applicable national grace/exception provisions in Chapter 1 Section 1.10 and exclude qualifying disclosures from prior-art assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternatives / Markush claims anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a claim contains alternatives (e.g., Markush claims), any alternatives disclosed in the prior art are anticipated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If prior art discloses any listed alternative, that alternative anticipates the claim inasmuch as it falls within the claimed alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relevant date for assessing prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'relevant date' for considering prior art means the national filing date or international filing date or the date of priority when a valid priority claim exists; different claims or alternatives may have different relevant dates depending on priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty separately for each claim or claim part with potentially different relevant dates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterisation of the Person Skilled In the Art (PSIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PSIA is a hypothetical person with ordinary skill who is aware of common general knowledge at the relevant date and has access to prior art cited in the search report and routine means for experimentation; in some advanced or specialized fields consider a group rather than a single person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume PSIA has normal experimental capabilities and access to cited art; adapt the PSIA construct for team-based or highly specialized technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enabling disclosure requirement in prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: The prior art disclosure must enable a PSIA to carry out the claimed invention; a mere mention (e.g., name/formula of a compound) is not considered known unless the document and general knowledge enable its preparation or separation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat non-enabling prior art as not destroying novelty though it may still be relied upon for inventive-step analysis; for patent documents enablement is ordinarily inferred, but for non-patent literature check enablement carefully.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combining documents to destroy novelty (single vs multiple references)
rubrics_metrics.description: As a rule, a single prior art is considered for novelty; however, if a primary document explicitly refers to a second document available to the public on the primary's publication date, teachings of the second may be incorporated. It is permissible to rely on additional documents to show that the primary's disclosure was sufficient. It is not permissible to combine separate items from different embodiments in the same document unless combination is specifically suggested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally require single-reference anticipation; permit incorporation by reference and use of secondary documents as evidence of sufficiency, but avoid impermissible piecing-together of disparate embodiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for anticipation of ranges
rubrics_metrics.description: Guiding principles: (1) a specific example in prior art within a claimed range anticipates the range; (2) prior-art ranges touching/overlapping the claimed range may anticipate if disclosed with 'sufficient specificity' (case-by-case); (3) a narrow claimed range within a broader prior-art range may still be novel if selection is sufficiently specific and yields unexpected results; (4) prior art teaching values very close but not overlapping do not anticipate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'sufficient specificity' based on facts; consider examples and jurisdictional guidelines (Indonesia, Singapore, Viet Nam) and selection-invention doctrine when narrow ranges show special effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second medical use and treatment-exclusion considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: For pharmaceuticals, some AMS exclude product patents in certain countries, and claims in the form 'Use of substance X for the treatment of disease Y...' may be regarded as relating to a method for treatment explicitly excluded from patentability in AMS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess national law on product patents and exclusions for methods of treatment; consider permitted claim forms for second medical use where allowed (text notes that many AMS allow second medical use except Viet Nam).
